extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, judges, and law students studying infringement doctrine
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and explains legal tests and standards for patent infringement across manufactures, compositions, processes (arts), machines, and designs — including what counts as 'use', the required degree of identity, and special rules for designs and materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: License conditioned on payment — unauthorized use is infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: If a license to use is conditioned on the payment of money, the use without such payment will be an infringement of the patent, giving the United States courts jurisdiction, and may be enjoined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statement (with cases cited) that using under a conditional license without paying breaches the patentee's rights and supports injunctive relief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement of a manufacture or composition — making, using, selling, importing
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent for a 'manufacture' will be infringed by the same acts as a patent for a composition of matter, that is, by making, using, or selling the thing itself, or by importing it from a foreign country where it has been made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treats the vendible/tangible product as the subject of the patent; citations and examples (paint, medicine, stove, fabric) show the patent covers the physical article.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent on product generally covers the process of making it
rubrics_metrics.description: When the subject-matter is the thing produced, the patent will generally also cover the process of making it; a 'using' of the invention may consist in putting it in practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains overlap between product and process rights for products that are the subject of patents; supports treating making/practising process as part of infringement inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use by consumption (perishable/consumable articles) may be infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: In regard to classes of things which perish in the using, the use by which they are consumed may be regarded as a violation of the patent right; the party who sells or gives the article to be consumed may be held responsible for using it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognizes practical limits: consumer who unknowingly buys a counterfeit patented medicine might technically be 'using' it but public policy concerns arise; still, in strictness consumption can be an infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sale to agent and circumstantial evidence of infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: The sale of a patented article to an agent of the patentee employed to make the purchase on account of the patentee is not in itself an infringement; but, when accompanied by other circumstances, it may be submitted to the jury as evidence of infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citation: Byam v. Bullard; use sales to agent as evidentiary fact, not automatically dispositive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using a patented machine includes producing its intended effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the subject of the patent is a machine, the using is altogether prohibited by the statute, because it intends to vest in the patentee the full enjoyment of the fruits of his invention, both in the practice of making the machine and of producing the effect or result intended to be produced by it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes that operating a patented machine to achieve its intended result constitutes 'use' and is within scope of exclusive right.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manufacturing under order (third-party contractors) can constitute infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: Where an order is given to defendants by a third person to manufacture a patented article on a model furnished by him, and the order is executed, the defendants were held guilty of an infringement, although they had no knowledge of the plaintiff's patent when they began to execute the order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bryce v. Dorr and other cases: liability can attach to manufacturers who execute orders even without initial knowledge; acting as maker is actionable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement of an art (process) — practicing the art is using
rubrics_metrics.description: Where an art is the subject-matter of a patent, the patent will be infringed by exercising or practising the same art, which will constitute a 'using' of the invention or discovery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: But courts may doubt whether mere use for a different purpose, with rejection of the valuable result of the process (i.e., accidental/ancillary results), constitutes infringement (illustrated by sewage deodorization case).

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary test — identity or substantial identity between the two things
rubrics_metrics.description: If the two things, one of which is said to be an infringement upon the other, are the same, there is an infringement; if they are different, there is not. The decisive inquiry is what kind and degree of resemblance constitute the identity the patent law designates as an infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledges difficulty of defining degree of resemblance; courts look to particular facts and cases to determine 'substantial identity'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of an invention — what counts as the 'principle' vs mere form
rubrics_metrics.description: What constitutes 'principle' of an invention is subtle: ascertain the result to be obtained, and whatever is essential to that object, independent of the mere form and proportions, may generally be considered as the principles of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quotes judges (Treadwell v. Bladen, Story, etc.) explaining that 'principle' means modus operandi or peculiar device of producing an effect, not abstract elementary truths of science.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design-infringement test (Circuit Court view) — expert side-by-side substantial identity
rubrics_metrics.description: The proper test in designs is substantial identity judged not by casual observers but by a person versed in the business of designs in the particular trade, accustomed to compare such designs intelligently one with another, and who sees and examines the articles side by side.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Circuit Court (Gorham Co. v. White, as cited) endorsed substantial identity as in machinery but measured by a skilled observer; view later rejected by Supreme Court.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design-infringement test (Supreme Court view) — ordinary observer/same appearance
rubrics_metrics.description: If, in the eye of an ordinary observer giving such attention as a purchaser usually gives, two designs are substantially the same — the resemblance being such as to deceive such an observer, inducing him to purchase one supposing it to be the other — the patented design is infringed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supreme Court rejects expert-only test; focuses on resultant effect/appearance to ordinary purchasers and whether resemblance deceives them; includes discussion that identity of appearance, not means used to produce it, is controlling for designs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantial identity defined — copy with only immaterial variations
rubrics_metrics.description: An infringement involves substantial identity; it is a copy of the thing described in the specification of the patentee, either without variation, or with only such variations as are consistent with its being in substance the same thing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cannot be fully stated in general terms; courts rely on individual case illustrations. Walton v. Potter quoted: look to whether defendants have availed themselves of plaintiff's invention in reality, substance, and effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Material/composition limitations affect scope — claiming material can limit infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: When a patentee specifies a particular material (e.g., patent covers a superior material), use of a different or inferior material by a defendant may or may not constitute infringement; if the patentee covered material specifically, employing a different material may avoid liability, especially if patentee had rejected the alternative as valueless.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aiken v. Bemis: whether difference is immaterial or a deliberate limiting choice by patentee affects infringement analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Machine-infringement rule — same service/effect by same or substantially same mode
rubrics_metrics.description: If the invention be a machine, it will be infringed by a machine which incorporates in its structure and operation the substance of the invention; that is, by an arrangement of mechanism which performs the same service or produces the same effect in the same way, or substantially the same way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wyeth v. Stone, Odiorne v. Winkley, and other instructions: focus on whether effect is produced substantially by the same mode of operation and combination of powers; mere colorable differences or slight improvements do not avoid infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combinations and successive improvements — limits on claiming entire machine
rubrics_metrics.description: A later inventor cannot claim a patent for the whole of a machine which embraces inventions previously made by others; each inventor is entitled to his own invention and no more; a patent that improperly includes earlier inventions may be void.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by hypothetical watch example and Wyeth/Odiorne discussion — relevant to both infringement and validity inquiries when multiple prior contributors exist.
